title: Washington AI Laws

reading.body:
Washington's only AI law on the books regulates companion chatbots, not the data centers or power that dominate AI's physical buildout.

The law, HB2225, passed on 2026-03-24. It requires operators to disclose that a chatbot is artificial and not human, with recurring notifications rather than a one-time label. It adds protections for minors, restricting sexually explicit content and manipulative engagement techniques. It also requires operators to keep protocols for detecting and responding to suicidal ideation or self-harm, and to disclose those protocols publicly.

The pattern is narrow and consumer-facing. The obligations fall on the operator of a conversational product, and they concern what the system says and how it engages a person, not how it is trained or where it runs. For AI specifically, this is a reminder that state AI regulation so far can attach to the interface layer, far from the compute, buildings, and power that this site treats as the binding constraints on scaling. A chatbot disclosure rule does not touch a data center's interconnection queue or its electricity contract.

What this does not tell the reader: it says nothing about Washington's treatment of frontier model training, data center siting, or grid load. One law is a thin basis for characterizing a state's posture, and the data covers only enacted text, not pending bills or agency rules.
